selection_rule: Lowest validation MAE (2022); test results are reported only.
core_explanation: Ranking on the same test weeks: Stacking (RF+XGB+LGBM+CatBoost -> Ridge: MAE 14.23, +4.8% vs naive), then Bagging (Random Forest: MAE 14.52, +2.9% vs naive), then Boosting (XGBoost: MAE 16.51, -10.4% vs naive). The naive rule scores 14.95.

Bagging (Random Forest) averages hundreds of deep trees, which removes noise (lower variance): it is 18% more accurate than naive in normal weeks (6.07 vs 7.43) and close to naive in outbreak weeks (21.39 vs 21.06).

Boosting (XGBoost) adds shallow trees one at a time to remove bias. It fits calm weeks best (normal-week MAE 5.93) but under-forecasts surges (outbreak-week MAE 25.11, average error -20.4 cases). The cause is the log-cases target, not boosting itself: the same XGBoost trained on raw cases scores MAE 14.37 (+3.9% vs naive) with an outbreak error of only -6.3. Log-cases was chosen because it won on the calm 2022 validation year.

Stacking learns how to combine Random Forest, XGBoost, LightGBM and CatBoost. Their errors are 98% correlated, so it cannot gain much from diversity, but its meta-learner weights sum to 1.05, lifting forecasts slightly and correcting part of the shared under-forecast (outbreak-week MAE 20.37, the lowest of the three).

family_explanations.Baseline: Simple rules with no learning (e.g. next week = this week); every model must beat them.
family_explanations.Bagging: Many deep trees trained on random resamples of the data and averaged, which lowers variance.
family_explanations.Boosting: Small trees added one after another, each correcting the previous errors, which lowers bias.
family_explanations.Stacking: A meta-model learns how much to trust each base model's forecast.
family_explanations.Neural net: A small neural network (MLP) that learns smooth patterns and can forecast above past values.
family_explanations.Hybrid: Two different kinds of model combined: SARIMA + Random Forest, or Random Forest + neural network.

key_findings: Next week usually looks like this week, so the simple rule 'next week = this week' is a tough benchmark (test MAE 14.95 cases per region-week). Recent case counts carry about 85% of the model's reasoning; weather about 8%, strongest for rain and humidity 5 and 7 weeks earlier.

Bagging was the most reliable single family: Random Forest and Extra Trees beat the naive rule by about 3% (MAE 14.51), being 19% more accurate in normal weeks while staying about level with naive in outbreak weeks.

Boosting was the most accurate in calm weeks (normal-week MAE 5.89-6.33) but under-predicted the 2023-2026 surges, ending 3-24% worse than naive. A test showed why: trained on the log of cases, LightGBM scored MAE 18.59; trained on raw cases it scored 14.60, because the log transform pulls forecasts of big outbreaks down.

Stacking improved on every single model on test (MAE 14.23, +4.8% vs naive) even though the base models' errors were 98% correlated: its meta-learner weights add up to 1.05, slightly scaling forecasts up, which offsets the trees' tendency to under-forecast outbreaks. Simple averaging (voting) did not (-4.4%).

The best test result came from a hybrid: 80% Random Forest + 20% neural network (MAE 14.19, +5.1% vs naive). The two make opposite mistakes in outbreaks (the forest forecasts too low, the network can over-shoot), so blending them cancels part of the error. SARIMA + Random Forest on the national total also beat naive (+4.0%) while each part alone did not.
dashboard_findings: **The naive rule is hard to beat.** Dengue is persistent, so 'next week = this week' already scores MAE 14.95; recent case counts drive about 85% of every model's forecast.
**Bagging reduced variance.** Random Forest averages hundreds of deep trees, making it 18% more accurate than naive in normal weeks and +2.9% overall.

**Boosting reduced bias but missed outbreaks.** XGBoost was the most accurate in calm weeks (MAE 5.93) but under-forecast surges (-10.4% overall); trained on raw instead of log cases it would have scored 14.37.

**Stacking helped a little.** The base models' errors were 98% correlated, so there was little diversity to exploit; stacking still came out best of the three strategies (+4.8%) because its meta-learner lifted the shared under-forecast of outbreaks. A Random Forest + neural-network hybrid was best overall (+5.1%).

**Record outbreaks are hard for trees.** Trees cannot forecast above the values they were trained on, and every model lagged the 2023–2026 surges (55% of test weeks were outbreak weeks). Only 0.4% of test weeks exceeded a region's training maximum, so the bigger problem was that outbreak-level weeks were rare in the training years.
hybrid_notes: RF + SARIMA, national weekly total: hybrid MAE 202 cases/week vs naive 211 (+4.0%); SARIMA alone -2.0%, RF alone -17.9%. SARIMA supplies the seasonal level, the forest corrects what SARIMA misses.
RF + SARIMA, Colombo: nothing beat naive (hybrid -6.6%); Colombo's sudden 2026 surge was faster than any model could follow one week ahead.
RF + ANN weighted average: weight 0.80 on the forest, tuned on 2022. Test MAE 14.19 (+5.1% vs naive), the best of all models on test; the ANN alone scored -16.7%.
RF -> ANN (forest forecast as an extra network input): -9.5% vs naive; feeding one model into the other amplified errors in outbreaks instead of cancelling them.
why_best: No single family dominated, so the answer has two parts. Among single model families, bagging (Random Forest / Extra Trees) was the most reliable: averaging hundreds of deep trees keeps forecasts close to recent case levels while removing noise, beating the naive rule by about 3%. Overall, the best test results came from combining models whose mistakes partly cancel: stacking (+4.8%) and the Random Forest + neural network hybrid (+5.1%). Boosting was best in calm weeks but worst in outbreaks, because trained on log-cases it under-forecasts surges. The deployed model, Extra Trees, was chosen in advance by the 2022 validation error; 2022 was a calm year, so validation could not fully separate the models' outbreak behaviour.
